Java.title: String immutability
Java.question: Why does calling text.concat("!") without assigning the returned value leave a Java String variable unchanged?
options: String objects are immutable and concat returns a new String
The JVM ignores punctuation during concatenation
Java.explanation: String is immutable: methods that appear to modify it return a new object. Assign the result, or use StringBuilder when repeated mutation is required.

Java.title: HashMap lookup
Java.question: What is the expected average-time complexity of get(key) in a well-distributed Java HashMap?
Java.explanation: With a good hash distribution, the key maps directly to a small bucket, so lookup is O(1) on average. Pathological collisions can make the worst case slower.

Java.title: Method overloading
Java.question: Java chooses among overloaded methods primarily at which time?
options: At compile time from the declared argument types
When the class loader unloads the class
Java.explanation: Overloading is compile-time polymorphism. The compiler selects the most specific applicable signature using the declared types and conversion rules.

Java.title: Interface defaults
Java.question: If a class implements two interfaces that provide conflicting default methods with the same signature, what must the class do?
options: Override the method and resolve the conflict explicitly
Java.explanation: Java cannot choose between unrelated default implementations. The implementing class must override the method and may call a chosen default with InterfaceName.super.method().

Java.title: Try-with-resources
Java.question: Which objects can be managed automatically by a try-with-resources statement?
options: Any object with a finalize method
Java.explanation: Resources declared in try-with-resources must implement AutoCloseable (or Closeable). Java closes them in reverse declaration order even when an exception occurs.

Java.title: equals and hashCode
Java.question: What contract must a Java class follow when it overrides equals?
options: Unequal objects must have different hash codes
Equal objects must return the same hash code
hashCode must always return a unique number
equals may change while an object is in a HashSet
Java.explanation: Objects considered equal must produce the same hash code. Unequal objects may collide, but stable equality and hash values are important while keys are stored in hash-based collections.

Java.title: Volatile fields
Java.question: What guarantee does volatile provide for a Java field?
options: Writes become visible to other threads that subsequently read the field
The field can never be changed
Access is restricted to one thread
Java.explanation: volatile establishes visibility and ordering guarantees between threads. It does not make compound operations such as count++ atomic; use synchronization or atomic classes for that.

Java.title: Stream evaluation
Java.question: When do most intermediate Java Stream operations such as map and filter perform their work?
options: Only when a terminal operation consumes the stream
Java.explanation: Intermediate stream operations are lazy. They build a pipeline that is traversed when a terminal operation such as collect, reduce, or forEach is invoked.

Java.title: Synchronized monitor
Java.question: Which monitor is acquired by a synchronized instance method?
options: The Class object for every call
Java.explanation: A synchronized instance method locks this. A static synchronized method instead locks the corresponding Class object.

Java.title: Records
Java.question: What is the main purpose of a Java record declaration?
options: Define a concise data carrier with generated accessors, equality, hash code, and representation
Run code in a separate process
Java.explanation: Records provide compact syntax for transparent data carriers. Their components are final references, and the compiler generates accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString.

DSA.title: Breadth-first search
DSA.question: Which traversal finds a minimum-edge path from a source in an unweighted graph?
DSA.explanation: BFS visits vertices layer by layer, so the first visit to a vertex uses the fewest edges. Its time is O(V + E) with an adjacency list.

DSA.title: Binary heap
DSA.question: What are the usual time bounds for inserting an item into a binary heap and removing its root?
DSA.explanation: Insertion bubbles an item upward and root removal pushes a replacement downward. Both traverse at most the heap height, O(log n).

DSA.title: AVL tree
DSA.question: Why does an AVL tree perform rotations?
options: To keep every key at the root
To restore a bounded height after updates
To convert the tree into a linked list
DSA.explanation: AVL rotations repair balance factors after insertion or deletion, keeping height O(log n) and therefore search, insert, and delete O(log n).

DSA.title: Disjoint-set union
DSA.question: Which two optimizations make a disjoint-set structure nearly constant time per operation?
options: Path compression and union by rank or size
DSA.explanation: Path compression flattens find paths, while union by rank/size prevents tall trees. A sequence of operations costs O(alpha(n)) amortized per operation.

DSA.title: Topological order
DSA.question: A topological ordering exists for which graph category?
DSA.explanation: A topological order requires every directed edge to go from an earlier to a later vertex, which is possible exactly when the directed graph has no cycle.

DSA.title: Dijkstra algorithm
DSA.question: Which edge restriction is required by the standard Dijkstra shortest-path algorithm?
options: The graph must be a tree
Every vertex must have even degree
DSA.explanation: Dijkstra finalizes the smallest tentative distance, a step that is valid only when later edges cannot reduce it through a negative weight.

DSA.title: Merge sort
DSA.question: Which statement best describes merge sort?
options: Unstable O(n²) time and O(1) space
Stable O(n log n) time with O(n) auxiliary array space in its usual array form
Average O(n) time for every input
DSA.explanation: Merge sort recursively sorts halves and merges them. The usual array implementation is stable, runs in O(n log n), and uses O(n) auxiliary storage.

DSA.title: Monotonic stack
DSA.question: Why can a monotonic stack find the next greater element for every array position in O(n) time?
options: It sorts the whole array first
Each element is pushed and popped at most once
It compares every pair in parallel
It uses a balanced tree for every element
DSA.explanation: The stack keeps unresolved indices in monotonic order. Although one item may pop several entries, each index enters and leaves the stack once, so total work is O(n).

DSA.title: Trie lookup
DSA.question: For strings over a fixed alphabet, what primarily determines trie insertion and prefix-search time?
options: The number of stored strings only
The length L of the queried string
The numeric value of each character
The height of a binary heap
DSA.explanation: A trie follows one edge per character, giving O(L) insertion and prefix lookup. Its memory cost can be high because nodes store child links.

DSA.title: Sparse graph storage
DSA.question: Which representation is usually most memory-efficient for a sparse graph?
options: A full V by V table of weights
One array containing every possible edge
DSA.explanation: An adjacency list stores vertices plus existing edges, using O(V + E) space, whereas an adjacency matrix always uses O(V²).

DBMS.title: First normal form
DBMS.question: What does First Normal Form primarily require?
options: Every table has exactly one row
Each column value is atomic rather than a repeating group
Every determinant is a candidate key
DBMS.explanation: 1NF requires rows and columns to form a relation with atomic values and no repeating groups. Higher normal forms address dependency anomalies.

DBMS.title: Second normal form
DBMS.question: Which dependency does Second Normal Form remove when a table has a composite key?
options: A full dependency on the whole key
A partial dependency on only part of the key
DBMS.explanation: A 2NF relation is in 1NF and each non-key attribute depends on the whole candidate key, not just one component of a composite key.

DBMS.title: Third normal form
DBMS.question: Which common anomaly does Third Normal Form target?
options: Transitive dependency of a non-key attribute through another non-key attribute
A primary key containing one column
Rows returned in no guaranteed order
DBMS.explanation: 3NF removes non-key-to-non-key transitive dependencies, reducing update, insertion, and deletion anomalies.

DBMS.title: ACID isolation
DBMS.question: What does the isolation property of a transaction aim to provide?
options: Concurrent transactions behave as though executed in a valid serial order
DBMS.explanation: Isolation controls interference among concurrent transactions. Depending on the configured level, the result approaches or guarantees serializable execution.

DBMS.title: B-tree index
DBMS.question: Why is a B-tree-family index useful for database range queries?
options: It stores keys in ordered balanced pages
It scans every table row first
It removes the need for comparison operators
DBMS.explanation: B-trees remain shallow and ordered, supporting O(log n) navigation to the first key and efficient sequential scanning across a range.

DBMS.title: LEFT JOIN
DBMS.question: What does a LEFT JOIN return?
options: Only rows that match on both sides
Every row from the left table plus matching right rows, with NULLs when no match exists
DBMS.explanation: A LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves all left-side rows. Columns from the right side are NULL when the join condition finds no match.

DBMS.title: Deadlock detection
DBMS.question: In a wait-for graph, what indicates a transaction deadlock?
options: A vertex with no outgoing edge
DBMS.explanation: A directed cycle means each transaction in the cycle waits for a resource held by the next. The DBMS must abort or roll back at least one participant.

DBMS.title: Foreign key
DBMS.question: What is the main role of a foreign-key constraint?
options: Maintain referential integrity between related tables
DBMS.explanation: A foreign key restricts child values to existing referenced keys (or NULL when allowed), with configurable actions for parent updates and deletes.

DBMS.title: MVCC
DBMS.question: What is a key benefit of multi-version concurrency control?
options: Readers can often use a consistent snapshot without blocking writers
It guarantees every query uses an index
It removes all old row versions immediately
It prevents transactions from rolling back
DBMS.explanation: MVCC retains row versions so readers can observe a transactionally consistent snapshot while writers create newer versions, reducing read/write contention.

DBMS.title: Denormalization
DBMS.question: Why might a system deliberately denormalize a well-normalized schema?
options: To trade extra storage and update complexity for faster read queries
To guarantee no duplicate data exists
DBMS.explanation: Denormalization duplicates or precomputes data to reduce joins and speed reads. It adds storage and requires careful consistency maintenance on writes.

OS.title: Processes and threads
OS.question: Which statement correctly contrasts processes and threads?
options: Threads always have separate virtual address spaces
Threads in one process usually share an address space, while processes are isolated
OS.explanation: Processes normally have separate virtual address spaces. Threads within a process share code and heap but keep their own registers, stack, and scheduling state.

OS.title: Round-robin scheduling
OS.question: What mechanism distinguishes round-robin CPU scheduling?
options: Tasks run until completion with no preemption
Each ready task receives a bounded time quantum in cyclic order
The largest task always runs first
Only kernel threads may be scheduled
OS.explanation: Round robin is preemptive: a timer interrupts a task after its quantum and places it at the end of the ready queue when work remains.

OS.title: Deadlock conditions
OS.question: Which set contains all four Coffman conditions required for deadlock?
options: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait
OS.explanation: Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions simultaneously. Breaking any one of them prevents deadlock.

OS.title: Virtual memory
OS.question: What does virtual memory allow an operating system to provide?
options: Only one program can use RAM
Each process sees a protected logical address space that may exceed physical RAM
Every address directly names a disk sector
OS.explanation: The MMU maps virtual pages to physical frames or backing storage, giving isolation, flexible allocation, sharing, and an address space larger than resident RAM.

OS.title: Page fault
OS.question: When does a page fault occur?
options: A CPU instruction divides by zero
A referenced virtual page is not currently mapped with the required access
OS.explanation: A page fault traps to the OS because the page is absent or access is invalid. The OS may load a valid page, update mappings, or terminate an illegal access.

OS.title: Mutex purpose
OS.question: What is a mutex primarily used for?
options: Ensure only one thread at a time enters a protected critical section
OS.explanation: A mutex provides mutual exclusion around shared state. Correct locking prevents data races and preserves invariants.

OS.title: Context switch
OS.question: What must the OS do during a context switch between runnable threads?
options: Save the current execution state and restore another thread’s state
OS.explanation: The scheduler saves registers such as the program counter and stack pointer, updates bookkeeping, then restores the selected thread’s saved context.

OS.title: Starvation prevention
OS.question: How does aging help a priority scheduler?
options: Gradually raises the priority of jobs that wait a long time
Reduces every time quantum to zero
OS.explanation: Aging increases a waiting task’s priority over time so a continuous stream of higher-priority arrivals cannot postpone it forever.

OS.title: Atomic primitives
OS.question: Which hardware primitive is commonly used to build lock implementations?
OS.explanation: Atomic read-modify-write operations such as compare-and-swap let threads coordinate a lock state without an interruptible check-then-set race.

OS.title: Copy-on-write
OS.question: Why is copy-on-write efficient after fork?
options: Parent and child initially share physical pages until one writes
It immediately duplicates every memory page
It stores all process memory in CPU registers
OS.explanation: fork can share read-only mappings between parent and child. A write triggers a protected fault and copies only the modified page, saving time and memory.

Networks.title: Transport layer
Networks.question: Which protocols are best known as Internet transport-layer protocols?
Networks.explanation: TCP and UDP provide end-to-end transport over IP. TCP is reliable and connection-oriented; UDP is datagram-oriented with lower overhead.

Networks.title: DNS
Networks.question: What is the main function of the Domain Name System?
options: Translate domain names into resource records such as IP addresses
Networks.explanation: DNS is a distributed hierarchical naming system. Resolvers query records such as A, AAAA, MX, and CNAME and cache answers according to TTLs.

Networks.title: ARP
Networks.question: On a typical IPv4 LAN, what does ARP discover?
options: The MAC address associated with a local IPv4 address
The shortest route across the Internet
Networks.explanation: ARP broadcasts a local request for an IPv4 address and caches the owner’s link-layer address so Ethernet frames can be delivered.

Networks.title: TCP handshake
Networks.question: What is the normal order of the TCP three-way connection handshake?
Networks.explanation: The initiator sends SYN, the listener replies SYN-ACK, and the initiator acknowledges. The exchange synchronizes sequence numbers and confirms both directions.

Networks.title: Subnet mask
Networks.question: What does an IPv4 subnet mask identify?
options: Which address bits form the network prefix and which form the host portion
The TCP port used by DNS
The physical length of a cable
Networks.explanation: Mask bits set to one select the network prefix. Hosts compare masked addresses to decide whether a destination is local or requires a router.

Networks.title: HTTP status
Networks.question: What does HTTP status code 404 conventionally mean?
options: The request succeeded with no body
The requested resource was not found
The server permanently redirected the resource
Networks.explanation: 404 Not Found means the origin could not locate a current representation for the requested target. It does not by itself say whether the absence is temporary.

Networks.title: TLS
Networks.question: What security properties does a correctly validated TLS connection provide?
Networks.explanation: TLS negotiates encryption and integrity keys and authenticates the server certificate. Client authentication is optional.

Networks.title: Router layer
Networks.question: At which conceptual layer does an IP router primarily forward traffic?
Networks.explanation: Routers inspect destination IP prefixes and forward packets between networks, the core function of the network layer.

Networks.title: TCP slow start
Networks.question: What happens to the congestion window during the initial TCP slow-start phase when acknowledgments arrive normally?
options: It grows rapidly, approximately doubling each round-trip time
It remains exactly one segment forever
It is controlled only by DNS
Networks.explanation: Each acknowledgment increases the window, producing roughly exponential growth per RTT until a threshold or congestion signal changes the algorithm.

Networks.title: UDP behavior
Networks.question: Which description best matches UDP?
options: Connectionless datagrams without built-in delivery or ordering guarantees
A reliable byte stream with retransmission
Networks.explanation: UDP adds ports and a checksum to IP datagrams but does not establish a connection, retransmit losses, order packets, or control congestion for the application.
